commentary: 24 dossiers of ancient text, later French historical scholarship and clearly identified secondary Gihr quotation; these are controls and cross-references to first-batch records rather than 24 additional fully reviewed liturgical slots.

criticalHolds.note: De sacramentis attributed to Ambrose in manuscript tradition; ancient/modern scholarship debates authorship. Cite as late-4th-century text transmitted under Ambrose, not proven Mass by St Ambrose or the whole historical Roman Canon.
Hebrew Genesis 14:18 'brought forth' cannot itself prove sacrificial offering of bread/wine, despite Catholic patristic interpretation and wording in Roman Canon.
Early text has heavenly-altar angelic petition and named patriarchal sacrifices in one form; received Canon reverses and separates the distinct material. No assumption of unchanging prayer text.
Google Books verifies the printed 1902 text/TOC; 2021 Angelus cites excerpts. Treat as SECONDARY_QUOTATION pending full printed-page validation; no chapter-level interpretation cleared.
DTC 1929 reconstructions about time of elevations, epiclesis, Gelasian and Gregorian reforms must be compared with independent manuscript-based modern scholarship.
De sacramentis 4.5.25 proves an early Communion Amen response in its historical setting; this does not resolve the 1962 low-vs-sung-Mass assignment of every specific response.
Patristic types and heavenly liturgy must not create invented historical routes, positions or cinematic claims. Artistic association cannot be promoted as documentary geography.

dossiers.title: Heavenly altar precedes naming sacrifices in earlier witness
dossiers.carefullyQualifiedClaim: In De sacramentis IV.6.27 the appeal that the offering be received at the heavenly altar through angels occurs in one continuous petition before Abel/Abraham/Melchizedek. In received Canon the prayers are separated, reordered, and use singular angel language. These must be represented as textual development, not a single unaltered fourth-century wording.

dossiers.title: Hebrew original means brought out, not explicitly sacrificed

Distinguish philology, interpretation and Roman Canon's explicit offering language.
